item.title: Today, In Short
item.description:
I grew up watching Nick Jonas and his brothers on Disney Channel. (“Camp Rock,” anyone?) Now, the 33-year-old is carving his own path, dabbling across mediums outside of music. He’s starring in “Power Ballad” alongside Paul Rudd, which is in theaters now.

Read more.

Primaries: The votes are still being counted in California. Three candidates are locked in a tight race for two spots in the November election for governor, and the current mayor of Los Angeles could end up in a runoff against a Republican reality star.

More on the primaries: In Iowa, President Trump’s pick for governor lost his race, and a progressive candidate prevailed in New Jersey. Here are four takeaways from the other races.

Middle East: An Iranian drone attack damaged a passenger terminal at Kuwait’s international airport and killed one person. Read the latest news.

Betting: Federal authorities are said to be investigating whether former Representative George Santos engaged in insider trading by placing bets on Kalshi, a prediction market, about his own appearance at the State of the Union address.

Fired: CBS News fired Scott Pelley of “60 Minutes” after months of tensions between the staff and Bari Weiss, the network’s editor in chief. This week, Pelley accused Weiss of “murdering” the longstanding news program.

Two things you didn’t really need to know but now do:

Beans, beans, they make you fart, but beans can also be … sexy? That’s what Violet Witchel wants you to think, at least. She’s behind the viral Dense Bean Salad, a food trend I’ve seen on my TikTok feed for years. Now, she’s doing pop-ups. Each “D.B.S.” will cost between $15 and $22.

Some TikTokers are processing their grief by posting about their experiences with unimaginable losses. These grief influencers use hashtags like #grieftok and #lifeafterloss, and have amassed huge followings.

Regular N.B.A. merch was not cutting it for Danielle Snyder. So, before attending her first N.B.A. game, she chopped up one of her husband’s old Warriors jerseys, stitched it back together on a white T-shirt in a patchwork fashion and bedazzled it. Her D.I.Y. project has become a lucrative business called DannijoPro, which she runs alongside her sister.

The WAGs have noticed.

Pasta salad is my go-to lunch, just ask my work bestie. I made this roasted zucchini one over the weekend, and the sunflower seeds added an amazing crunch. Next time, I’m adding feta.

Make this!

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. Write to us at inshort@nytimes.com. See you tomorrow! — Matt

item.title: Man Charged With Hate Crimes Over Swastika Flag Flown on N.Y.U. Campus
item.description:
A man was arrested on Tuesday in relation to an episode during New York University’s graduation celebrations in which a flag with two swastikas and a Star of David flew above a campus building, according to court documents.

The man, Alexander Stepnowsky, is charged with one count of hate crime burglary, two counts of hate crime aggravated harassment and one count of criminal trespassing in a hate crime. He was a student at the school at the time, Wiley Norvell, a spokesman for N.Y.U., said in an interview. A LinkedIn profile that matches biographic information about Mr. Stepnowsky said he was a music technology student at the Steinhardt School of Culture, Education and Human Development — the building over which the flag flew.

According to court records, Mr. Stepnowsky was born in 2002.

Mr. Stepnowsky was identified over the course of an investigation conducted by the school and the New York Police Department Hate Crimes Task Force, Mr. Norvell said. The spokesman did not confirm whether Mr. Stepnowsky participated in the commencement ceremony or graduated with a degree.

The Police Department confirmed that Mr. Stepnowsky was arrested on the Lower East Side at 1:30 p.m. on Tuesday. Mr. Stepnowsky’s permanent address was in Fairfield, Conn., the police said. A lawyer for Mr. Stepnowsky, Vickie Mwitanti, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“The symbols that were represented are antisemitic and hateful to every person of conscience; this appalling act violated our sense of community and solidarity,” Mr. Norvell said in a statement. “In addition to criminal proceedings, we will immediately pursue our disciplinary procedures, which carry the most severe consequences.”

The investigation included analyzing badge swipes and examining camera footage, according to a university official familiar with the process.

On May 13, as N.Y.U. seniors and their families were participating in a commencement tradition known as Grad Alley, a block-party-style celebration, the Police Department began receiving calls reporting harassment.

When officers arrived on the scene, a man informed them that a flag had shown antisemitic imagery in the form of two swastikas next to a Star of David. The purple-and-white flag was styled in a way that resembled the many purple N.Y.U. flags flying on campus buildings.

The Steinhardt School was named for Michael and Judy Steinhardt in 2001 after they donated $10 million to N.Y.U. to support “faculty development, doctoral fellowships and research.”

Mr. Steinhardt, a billionaire, made his money on Wall Street before becoming a major donor to N.Y.U. as well as to Jewish philanthropies. A conservatory at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and a gallery at the Metropolitan Museum of Art bear their name, as well.

Mr. Steinhardt is one of the founders of Birthright Israel, which sends young Jewish people on free trips to Israel to bolster their connection to the country and their Jewish identity.
